title.en: The Passion Play of Osiris at Abydos
title.zh: 阿拜多斯奧西里斯受難劇

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (temple, processional way, and the plain of Peqer)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（神廟、巡行道與佩克爾平原）

texts.period: Annual play attested by the stele of I-kher-nefert, 12th Dynasty (c. 1900 BCE), reproducing Old Kingdom rites (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XIV, 'The Shrines, Miracle Play, and Mysteries of Osiris' (stele of I-kher-nefert, Berlin 1024)

summary.en: The earliest recorded drama in the world: at Abydos each year the death and resurrection of Osiris was acted — the god's boat attacked by the foes of Set, Ap-uat leading the defense, the Great Coming-forth of the dead god's body from the temple with wailing crowds and club-fights, the three-day search tracing the god by his footsteps, Thoth ferrying the body to the tomb at Peqer — with the official I-kher-nefert starring in every act.
summary.zh: 世上最古之戲劇：阿拜多斯歲歲搬演奧西里斯之死與復活——神舟遭塞特黨羽攻擊，阿普-烏阿特領眾禦敵；『大出遊』之日，亡神之體出廟，眾人號哭執杖相鬥；歷三日循神之足跡遍尋；托特以舟渡神體至佩克爾之墓——官員伊克赫爾-奈費爾特親歷每幕。

sensitivity.note: Ancient ritual drama; no living community restrictions. OCR text used with care; quotations cleaned of obvious OCR breaks.

passages.text: We know from the evidence of the inscriptions that such a play was performed at Abydos once a year under the Middle and New Empires, and it is only reasonable to assume that it reproduced all the essential features of the great annual festival of the god which was celebrated under the Ancient Empire. In religious matters at least the conservatism of the ancient Egyptians was absolute.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: The second portion of the inscription on the stele of I-kher-nefert is of very great importance, for it describes briefly the principal scenes in the Osiris play which was performed at Abydos annually. I-kher-nefert himself played a prominent part in this 'Mystery play', and he describes his own acts as follows: 'I performed the coming forth of Ap-uat when he set out to defend his father.' From this it is clear that in the XIIth dynasty Ap-uat was regarded as the son of Osiris, and that he acted the part of leader of Osiris's expedition, which was represented by a procession formed of priests and the ordinary people. Ap-uat walked in front, next came the boat containing the figure of the god and a company of priests or 'followers' of the god, and the rear was brought up by a crowd of people.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: 'I drove back the enemy from the Neshmet Boat, I overthrew the foes of Osiris.' The boat of the god was then attacked by a crowd of men who represented the foes of Osiris, and, as the god was defenceless, Ap-uat engaged them in combat, and beat them off, and the procession then continued on its way in the temple. 'I performed the Great Coming-forth, I followed the god in his footsteps.' This act was the greatest in the Osiris play, for it represented the 'coming forth' of Osiris from the temple after his death, and the departure of his body to his tomb. A solemn service was performed in the temple before the body was carried from it, and offerings were eaten sacramentally, and then the procession set out for the tomb.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: When it reached the door of the temple it was received by a mighty crowd of men and women who raised the death-wail, and uttered piercing shrieks and lamentations, and the women beat their breasts. Many of the men in the crowd were armed with sticks and staves, and some of them pressed forward towards the procession with the view of helping the god, whilst others strove to prevent them. Thus a sham fight took place, which, owing to the excitement of the combatants, often degenerated into a serious one. And, if Herodotus was correctly informed, this combat with clubs was waged with great obstinacy, and heads were broken... This fight was, of course, intended to represent the great battle which took place in prehistoric times between Set and Osiris, when Osiris was killed.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.

texts.canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XIV; stele of I-kher-nefert ed. Schaefer, Untersuchungen IV (1904)

narrative.en:
The Passion Play of Osiris is the oldest documented drama on earth: an annual staged death, battle, search, funeral, and victory, performed in the temple and processional ways of Abydos and attested by the autobiography of a man who acted in it.

THE SETTING. Abydos was the earthly centre of Osiris' kingdom: every tradition asserted that the god's head was buried there, the city's very symbol was the coffer-basket that held his head, and the rich bought burial beside him or had their mummies shipped upriver for a season's blessing. Under the 12th Dynasty the official I-kher-nefert, sent by King Usertsen III, rebuilt the god's shrine of sweet-smelling woods inlaid with gold, silver and lapis-lazuli, provided a new Neshmet Boat — a copy of the boat in which Osiris had sailed to the fatal meeting with Set — and established the office of 'Sa-mer-f', the god's 'beloved son', a priest with clean fingers who alone might dress the statue and touch the shrine's furniture. In his great stele (Berlin 1024) he records his own parts in the play.

THE ACTS. First, 'I performed the coming forth of Ap-uat when he set out to defend his father': Ap-uat, son and herald of Osiris, led a procession of priests and people, walking before the boat that carried the god's figure, the crowd streaming behind. Second, the boat was attacked by men playing the foes of Osiris; the god himself was defenceless, and Ap-uat engaged them and beat them off before the procession could continue. Third came the 'Great Coming-forth', the play's supreme act: the dead god's body left the temple for the tomb. Offerings were eaten sacramentally in the temple first; then the procession was received at the temple door by a mighty crowd of men and women wailing death-cries, the women beating their breasts; men armed with sticks and staves pressed in to help or hinder the god, and the sham fight — the re-fought battle of Netit where Set killed Osiris — often degenerated into real injury, just as Herodotus was told when he described the club-fight of Papremis.

THE SEARCH AND THE BURIAL. 'I followed the god in his footsteps' — the search party, led by I-kher-nefert, traced the dead god by his literal footprints across the battlefield, three days of wandering interrupted by renewed sham fights and great lamentations, until the body was found (a passage in the Pyramid Text of Pepi I names Isis and Nephthys as the finders, their cries of grief summoning Thoth, who came by boat and saw Isis caressing and embracing the body of her husband). Then 'I made the boat of the god to move': I-kher-nefert acted ferryman for Thoth, bringing the body from Netit; 'I provided the Boat of the Lord of Abydos called Kha-em-Maat (appearing in truth) with a cabin shrine', dressed the god in his festal apparel, fastened the two feathers of Maati on the coffin, tied a bandlet on the god's head, and placed a model of Set at his feet — and 'directed the ways of the god to his tomb in Peqer.'

PEQER. Excavations by Amelineau identified Peqer as the part of the Abydos plain called Umm el-Qa'ab, 'mother of pots', where the tombs of the First Dynasty kings stand — among them the tomb of King Khent, which the Egyptians of the New Kingdom firmly identified as the tomb of Osiris himself, and beside which a famous cenotaph of Osiris was made under the 22nd Dynasty. The play thus ends where the religion begins: the murdered god laid in the royal tomb, his faithful son following the ways of the god to the grave — and the whole city acting out, once a year, the death and rising that promised every Egyptian his own resurrection.

functions: Annual communal re-enactment of the Osiris cycle: murder, battle, search, funeral — Egypt's oldest recorded theatre
Pilgrimage economy of Abydos: burial and blessing absorbed from the god's shrine, mummies shipped upriver for a season
Sacral role of the official elite: I-kher-nefert records acting Ap-uat, ferryman of Thoth, and director of the god's ways to the tomb
Theology of the royal tomb: the First-Dynasty tomb of Khent at Peqer venerated as the grave of Osiris

title.en: The Mysteries of Osiris at Denderah: The Corn Mummy and the Sixteen Cakes
title.zh: 丹德拉奧西里斯秘祭：穀神像與十六塊祭餅

region.en: Denderah (Tentyris), Upper Egypt (temple reliefs of the Khoiak mysteries)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及丹德拉（坦提里斯，荷阿克秘祭浮雕神廟）

texts.period: Inscribed in the Ptolemaic temple of Denderah, reproducing rites attested from the Middle Kingdom (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XV, 'The Mysteries of Osiris at Denderah' (Mariette, Denderah IV, pls. 35-39)

summary.en: Egypt's agricultural resurrection rite in full: through the month of Khoiak, wheat and paste are kneaded in gold moulds into figures of Khenti-Amenti and Seker, watered daily, tied with four papyrus bands, dried in the sun; cakes are baked in the shapes of the sixteen members of Osiris; a sacred field is ploughed by black cows and sown with barley, dhura and flax; the Tet is raised on the last day, and for seven days the unburied god rests 'in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes' — the seven months in the womb of Nut.
summary.zh: 埃及農事復活祭全景：荷阿克月間，小麥與漿料於金模中揉成肯提-阿門提與塞克爾之像，日日灌水，以四條紙莎草帶束之，曬於日光；餅烤作奧西里斯十六肢體之形；聖田由黑牛犁耕，播大麥、高粱與亞麻；月末日舉起泰特柱——七日未葬之神『棲於門德斯之梧桐枝間』，象其七月在努特胎中。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple liturgy; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: At Mendes, a town closely connected with Busiris and the cult of Osiris, one kin of wheat and three kin of paste were placed in a large stone trough resting on four legs, and each day, from the 12th to the 21st day of Khoiak, three parts of a kin of water were poured from a gold goblet into the trough. On the 21st day the contents of the trough were taken out, and a measure of incense having been added to it, the whole was kneaded into the two halves of a gold mould for making the figure of Khenti-Amenti wearing the White Crown. The contents of the moulds were then taken out and tied together with four papyrus bands, and dried in the sun. At the eighth hour of the 22nd day of the month, the figure, and figures of gods and many lamps, were placed in boats, and taken by water to the tomb of the god, and there the figure of Khenti-Amenti was covered with a cloth, and afterwards buried.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XV.

passages.text: The moulds for the 'divine bread' were made of the wood of a red tree, and cakes were made from them in the forms of the sixteen members of Osiris, viz., his head, feet, bones, arms, heart, intestines, tongue, eye, fist, fingers, body, back, ears, backbone, ram's head, and hair. These cakes were put in a box, which was placed in a silver chest, and then set under the head of the god for protection.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.

passages.text: The Field of Osiris in which the sacred grain was to be sown was from 210 to 223 feet long; one end of it was sown with barley, its centre with dhura, and the other end with flax. The plough frame was made of two kinds of wood, and the ploughshare of black bronze; the cows which pulled it were black. The barley which grew in the Field was cut on the 20th day of Tobe, and was made into sacred cakes, the dhura was also made into cakes, and the linen made from the flax was used at the festival.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.

passages.text: On the 16th the festival of Osiris Khenti-Amenti was celebrated, and on that day the transformation of the god took place. On the 19th the figure of Seker was taken from its mould, and on that day Horus saw his father. On the 21st the figure of Osiris was taken from its mould; on the 24th Osiris was embalmed, and on the last day of the month the Tet was raised up, and Osiris was buried. For seven days, from the 24th to the last day of the month, Osiris remained unburied, and during these days he rested in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes. The seven days symbolize the seven months which he passed in the womb of his mother Nut, and the branches symbolize the goddess.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XV.

texts.language: Egyptian (temple inscription, Ptolemaic copy of older rites)
texts.canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (London, 1911), ch. XV, from Mariette, Denderah, vol. IV, plates 35-39

narrative.en:
The Denderah inscriptions preserve, in Ptolemaic dress, the fullest surviving liturgy of Egypt's central mystery: the annual making, burying and raising of Osiris in grain — the god as seed-corn.

BEGINNING: THE MONTH OF KHOIAK. On the 12th day of Khoiak, at Busiris, Mendes, Abydos, Memphis, and every sanctuary of Osiris, priests filled a stone trough with one kin of wheat and three or four kin of paste. Each day, from the 12th to the 21st, three parts of a kin of water were poured from a gold goblet into the trough — the god being watered like a field. On the 21st the swollen mass was kneaded into the two halves of a gold mould, one carrying the figure of Khenti-Amenti wearing the White Crown, and the halves, tied together with four papyrus bands, were set in the sun to dry: a corn-effigy of the god, the 'Osiris garden' in its most complete form. On the 22nd the figure, with figures of gods and many lamps, was placed in boats and taken by water to the god's tomb and buried.

MIDDLE: THE SIXTEEN MEMBERS AND THE SACRED FIELD. The same inscriptions regulate the 'divine bread': cakes baked in gold moulds of red-tree wood in the shapes of the sixteen members of Osiris — head, feet, bones, arms, heart, intestines, tongue, eye, fist, fingers, body, back, ears, backbone, ram's head, and hair — boxed, placed in a silver chest, and set under the head of the god. A second rite made the figure of Seker from an egg-shaped paste of earth from the town of Neter, dates, incense, fresh myrrh, spices and precious stones, pressed into a one-cubit gold mould and laid on a bed. And the Field of Osiris itself — 210 to 223 feet long — was ploughed by black cows drawing a plough of two woods with a black bronze share, one end sown with barley, the centre with dhura, the other with flax; the barley was cut on the 20th of Tobe and baked into the sacred cakes, and the flax became the linen of the festival.

END: HORUS SEES HIS FATHER, THE TET RAISED. The liturgy's final days stage the resurrection in ritual time: on the 16th, the 'transformation of the god' at the festival of Osiris Khenti-Amenti; on the 19th the figure of Seker left its mould — 'on that day Horus saw his father'; on the 21st the figure of Osiris itself was removed; on the 24th, embalmed; and on the last day of Khoiak the Tet, the backbone-pillar of Osiris, was raised up and the god was buried. For seven days the god remained unburied, resting 'in the branches of the sycamores of Mendes' — the seven days symbolizing the seven months he passed in the womb of his mother Nut, the branches symbolizing the goddess. The thirty-four festival boats with their 365 lamps, the peace chamber with its 'lord of silence' seated hand-on-mouth, and the funeral furniture drawn by yoked heifers — two obelisks, four coffers of the Four Sons of Horus with veils of blue, red, green and white, sixteen vulture plumes, and behind them a figure of the serpent Apep holding a knife to sever the cordage — completed a festival that enacted, in grain and gold, the whole theology of death-as-sowing.

functions: Agricultural resurrection liturgy: Osiris made in wheat and paste, watered, dried, buried and raised — death as sowing
Eucharistic cakes of the sixteen members eaten by the community of the god
Ritual calendar of Khoiak fixing the festival days of every Osiris sanctuary in Egypt
Theology of gestation: the god's seven unburied days equated with seven months in the womb of Nut

title.en: The Road to Abydos: Mummies Shipped for a Blessing
title.zh: 通往阿拜多斯之路：運棺受祝福

region.en: Abydos, Upper Egypt (the shrine of the god's head and its pilgrim plain)
region.zh: 埃及上埃及阿拜多斯（神首之祠與朝聖平原）

texts.period: Pilgrimage attested from the 12th Dynasty through the New Kingdom (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIV, the pilgrimage customs of Abydos

summary.en: Every good Egyptian's aim was 'to become an Osiris': the bodies of the wealthy who died far away were taken upriver to Abydos, laid by the shrine to absorb its beneficent emanations, and then returned home for burial — a traffic Budge compares with the modern Muslim festival of Shekh Sayyid al-Badawi at Tanta, where the dead are carried round the saint's tomb for a blessing.
summary.zh: 每個善者皆求『成為奧西里斯』：遠方亡故之富者，遺體必運往阿拜多斯，置於神祠之側以吸其靈福，而後運回故里安葬——伯奇以此比於今日坦塔之賽義德巴達維聖節：亡者繞聖墓一周以承福澤。

sensitivity.note: Ancient practice described in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. The comparison with a living Muslim festival is Budge's own observation and is quoted neutrally.

passages.text: It was believed that the dead who were buried at Abydos would be joined by the god to his company of followers in the Other World, that they would enjoy his protection, and that they would share in his offerings on festival days, and become partakers with him in immortality and everlasting happiness. The aim of every good man was to become an Osiris, and even in the Pyramid Texts we find it tacitly assumed that the kings for whom they were written had each become an Osiris, and the name of Osiris is actually prefixed to the names of some of them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: Very few Egyptians who were not natives of the neighbourhood could afford to buy tombs there and be buried in them, and the transport of mummified bodies from a great distance was both difficult and costly. Nevertheless, many men were so eager that their dead bodies should rest on the sacred soil of Abydos, and be near Osiris, if only for a short time, that it became the custom among the well-to-do classes to transport the mummies of their kinsfolk to Abydos so that they might absorb the beneficent emanations from the shrine of the god and be blessed by the influence of the place and its holy associations. These mummies were then taken back by river to the places whence they came, and buried in the tombs which had been provided for them.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: At Tanta I have seen dead bodies brought in and laid for a few moments by the tomb of the saint, or simply carried round his tomb-chamber, in order to obtain his blessing, and men and women stand motionless and silent by the iron gates of the tomb, merely to be blessed by its presence, and to gain a share in the spiritual benefits which are believed to emanate from it.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV, Budge's own observation at the festival of Shekh Sayyid al-Badawi, offered as a living parallel.

title.en: Peqer, Mother of Pots: The Tomb of a King Became the Tomb of a God
title.zh: 佩克爾，罐之母：王墓成神墓

region.en: Umm el-Qa'ab (Peqer), Abydos, Egypt (the First Dynasty royal necropolis)
region.zh: 埃及阿拜多斯烏姆卡阿布（佩克爾，第一王朝王陵）

texts.period: Royal tombs of the 1st Dynasty (c. 3000 BCE); identified as Osiris' tomb by New Kingdom pilgrims (Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XIV, the tomb of Osiris at Peqer

summary.en: Where was the god actually buried? The stele of I-kher-nefert answers 'Peqer' — and Amelineau's excavations identified Peqer with Umm el-Qa'ab, 'mother of pots', the Abydos plain holding the tombs of the First Dynasty kings, among them the tomb of King Khent which New Kingdom Egyptians firmly venerated as the tomb of Osiris himself, complete with a great cenotaph made under the 22nd Dynasty.
summary.zh: 神究竟葬於何處？伊克赫爾-奈費爾特碑答曰『佩克爾』——阿梅利諾之發掘證其即烏姆卡阿布（『罐之母』），阿拜多斯平原上第一王朝諸王之陵所在，其中有王肯特之墓，新王國埃及人篤信即奧西里斯之墓，且於二十二王朝為之立大神饋碑。

sensitivity.note: Ancient archaeology-myth; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Here we have a definite statement that the body of Osiris was buried, and that his tomb was situated in Peqer. But where was Peqer? This question has been satisfactorily answered by the extensive excavations of M. Amelineau at Abydos, who proved that Peqer is a portion of the great plain of Abydos which lies about a mile and a half from the temple of Osiris, and which is known to-day by the Arabic name of Umm al-Ka'ab, i.e., 'mother of pots,' because of the large quantity of pottery which has been found there. In this portion of the plain are found the tombs of the kings of the First dynasty, and among them is one, that of King Khent, which the Egyptians identified as the tomb of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XIV.

passages.text: There is not the least doubt about the fact of the identification, for numerous proofs have been obtained from the excavations that the place was called Peqer, and that under the New Empire the Egyptians were firmly convinced that the tomb of Khent was the tomb of Osiris. Moreover, the famous cenotaph of Osiris, which was made probably under the XXInd dynasty and which is described elsewhere, was found here by M. Amelineau.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XIV.

title.en: Isis of the Thousand Names: She Who Makes the Nile to Swell
title.zh: 千名之伊西斯：使尼羅漲溢者

region.en: Egypt under the New Empire (the pan-Egyptian cult of Isis)
region.zh: 新王國埃及（伊西斯全境崇拜）

texts.period: New Kingdom epithet lists (Brugsch, Thesaurus, cited in Budge 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XVI, 'The Goddess Isis'

summary.en: Under the New Empire Isis became the greatest goddess of Egypt, and her titles run from cosmic office — 'The female Ra. The Eye of Ra. The maker of the sunrise. She who vomiteth fire' — to nourishing intimacy — 'The Cow Heru-sekha, who bringeth forth all things. Who nourished the child Horus with her milk. Lady of bread. Lady of beer. Lady of Love' — down to the calendar: 'Consort of her father. Whose husband is the inundation of the Nile. Who maketh the Nile to swell in his season.'
summary.zh: 新王國之世，伊西斯為埃及至大女神，尊號自宇宙職司——『女拉也。拉之眼也。日出之創造者。吐火者也』——至哺育之親——『赫魯-塞哈母牛，生萬物者。以乳哺荷魯斯者。麵包之主。啤酒之主。愛之主』——直至曆法：『父之配偶。其夫乃尼羅之洪。於其季使尼羅漲溢者。』

passages.text: Under the New Empire Isis became, beyond all doubt, the greatest goddess in Egypt, and the following titles illustrate the estimation in which she was held throughout the land: 'She of many names. The Great One who is from the beginning. The divine one. The only one. The greatest of the gods and goddesses. The Queen of all the gods. The best beloved of all the gods. The prototype of all beings. Queen of goddesses and women. The female Ra. The female Horus. The Eye of Ra. The right eye of Ra (as Sothis). The star-crown of Ra-Horus. The Queen of the Dekan stars. Sothis, who openeth the New Year.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XVI (Brugsch, Thesaurus).

passages.text: 'The lady of heaven. The holy one of heaven. Light-giver in heaven with Ra. She of the beams of gold. The golden one. The most brilliant goddess. Lady of the north wind. The Queen of earth. The mightiest of the mighty. The mighty one on the earth of Keb. The Queen of the South and North. Lady of the solid earth. She who vomiteth fire. Blazing flame. She who filleth the Tuat with good things. The mother of the god Horus, the Mighty Bull. The Cow Heru-sekha, who bringeth forth all things. Who nourished the child Horus with her milk. Bestower of life. Lady of life. Creatress of green things.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI.

passages.text: 'Lady of bread. Lady of beer. Lady of abundance. Lady of joy and gladness. Lady of Love. Who delivereth to the king his rank, without whom no king can exist. Mistress of spells. Weaver and fuller. Daughter of Keb. Child of Nut. First royal wife of Ra. Consort of her father. Whose son is the lord of the earth. Whose husband is the lord of the deep. Whose husband is the inundation of the Nile. Who maketh the Nile to swell and overflow. Who maketh the Nile to swell in his season.' The last-mentioned titles of the goddess refer to Isis-Sothis, whose appearance in the sky indicated the immediate advent of the inundation of the Nile, and warned men to be ready to begin the agricultural labours of a new year.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XVI, with the closing explanation.

title.en: The Circumcision Rite: The Oldest Operation in Sculpture
title.zh: 割禮之儀：浮雕中最古之手術

region.en: Sakkarah, Egypt (the 6th-Dynasty tomb relief of the circumcision)
region.zh: 埃及薩卡拉（第六王朝墓室割禮浮雕）

texts.period: Relief in a 6th-Dynasty tomb at Sakkarah (c. 2300-2200 BCE); Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6, 'Circumcision'

summary.en: A ritual-origin record from the edge of the mythic: the mummified bodies prove circumcision general at all periods in Egypt; the oldest known representation of the operation is a 6th-Dynasty relief at Sakkarah where a priest performs it; a 'god of circumcision' appears in the Pyramid Text of Teta — and Budge argues the rite originated as an offering made to the gods of virility, as it still is among many African tribes.
summary.zh: 禮儀緣起記錄：木乃伊證割禮於埃及歷代通行；其最古圖像乃薩卡拉第六王朝墓中浮雕，由祭司執刀；泰塔金字塔文中已見『割禮之神』——伯奇論其本為獻予陽剛之神之祭品，如今日非洲諸族所行。

sensitivity.note: Ancient rite discussed in Budge 1911; no living community restrictions. Tagged 'ritual-origin' (topic 5); see ledger note on motif mapping.

passages.text: The mummified bodies of the ancient Egyptians which are available for examination prove that circumcision was general at all periods in Egypt. As, however, the texts say little or nothing about the ceremony itself, or its significance, we must assume that it had no religious importance, at least in Dynastic times, and that, if the earlier inhabitants of the Nile Valley ever regarded it as an act of worship, this view of it was ignored by their descendants or forgotten. Originally, circumcision must have had a religious significance, and there is little doubt that the portion cut from the body of the boy was regarded as an offering which was made to one or other of the gods of virility or generation, just as it is to-day among many of the tribes of Africa.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. II (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6.

passages.text: A representation of the performance of circumcision, probably the oldest known, is found on a relief in a tomb at Sakkarah, and it dates from the period of the VIth dynasty. The act is performed by a priest, but whether this official was a member of the boy's family, or a professional priest, cannot be said. A god of circumcision appears to be mentioned in the text of Teta (VIth dynasty), but in exactly what connection is not clear.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. XXIV, sec. 6.
